prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and the experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I opened with the IceCube neutrino candidate (B003) first and the topological-insulator candidate (B039) only fifth, and I have to be honest that the opening ballots do not support my ordering. Five of eight members, including the three whose own fields are closest to condensed matter, atomic theory and materials physics, place B039 in their top two or put it first. The case is strong on the criteria that matter: a new classification of electronic phases by band topology rather than symmetry breaking, a clean theory-to-experiment chain (Kane and Mele's Z2 invariant and quantum spin Hall proposal in 2005, then the observation of edge transport in HgTe wells by Molenkamp's group in 2007), independent confirmation across materials and techniques for about two decades, and an influence that has spread to photonics, cold atoms and device concepts. As an experimentalist I find the decisive experimental confirmation particularly persuasive: this is not a prediction awaiting a test. Recognition now would be timely, arguably overdue, and it complements rather than repeats the 2016 prize, which honoured topological phase transitions and topological phases in particular models, not the time-reversal-invariant band-structure topology of real materials. I therefore move B039 to the front of my preferred configuration, while stating plainly that this is a change of view caused by colleagues' evidence and not a pre-existing preference of mine.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The supplied credit omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe proposal is what directed the experiment, and it omits the three-dimensional topological-insulator work (Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, Hasan and others). Zhang is deceased, which cannot be repaired by adding a name, and a three-person limit means that any version of this prize leaves out people with real claims. The citation I propose is deliberately scoped to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant so that it matches the three names without implying that the whole field of topological insulators is credited. The second reservation is that this is the third prize in two decades on topology in condensed matter if the 2016 prize and the quantum Hall precedent are counted, so the committee should be able to state clearly what is new. A further, smaller reservation is that practical applications remain limited, so the case rests on conceptual and experimental impact.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B039 first as a clean theory-to-experiment chain and raises two issues: whether the prize should centre on 2D quantum spin Hall or on 3D topological insulators, and the risk of splitting this field across B039 and another candidate.
responses.response: I agree that the boundary must be fixed before we draft a citation, and I would fix it at the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant. That is the part where the three supplied names are most defensible: Kane and Mele for the invariant, Molenkamp for the experiment. If we widen the scope to 3D materials we immediately need Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan and the prize cannot be fairly allocated within three names. I do not share your confidence that the credit is coherent as it stands, because the BHZ proposal that guided Molenkamp's experiment is absent. Your point about not splitting the field is right, and it is a reason to keep this as one prize part, not to pair it with a second condensed-matter part.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock (B022) first as a clean and powerful idea with excellent timing, and places B039 only eighth, citing his lesser ability to judge condensed-matter details and the unfinished credit for Zhang, Bernevig, Hughes, Fu and Moore.
responses.response: I take the clock case seriously and keep B022 as my first alternative: the two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist and the independent comparisons are convincing. I would resist the argument that timing is excellent because the redefinition of the second is approaching. A pending redefinition is a reason to wait, not a maturity milestone we are missing, and the same maturity can be argued for topological insulators, which have two decades of independent confirmation. I share your attribution worry about B039 and think it is the real weakness, but it is a problem of allocation inside a clearly discovered phenomenon, whereas the clock candidate carries a different risk, that it is seen as a refinement of the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. Where you and I differ is on how heavily to weigh that overlap; I weigh it less than you do, but I cannot call it settled.

responses.point: Danielsson also ranks the IceCube candidate B003 first, as a secure discovery that opened a new window, while noting that the single credited name under-represents a collaboration-scale discovery.
responses.response: We are the only two members who ranked B003 first, and I should say plainly that this is thin support. I do not withdraw the science: the diffuse flux is secure and neutrino astronomy is real. But we both flagged the same attribution problem, and I now think it is disqualifying for this year in a way it would not be for a candidate with a defensible multi-name credit. A single-laureate prize for a discovery that rests on AMANDA, DUMAND, Baikal and a large IceCube collaboration risks an award that the community regards as unfair, and no member other than the two of us put it in the top five. I would keep it as a second alternative, and I would expect it to return with a broader credit list or after a second detector confirms the flux.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first and B039 second, describing the latter as a natural complement to the 2016 topological-phase prize that extends it to time-reversal-invariant systems.
responses.response: I agree with your framing of the 2016 relationship and I would use it in the citation discussion, because it answers the objection that the committee has already honoured topology. Where I qualify your view is on the claim that the allocation is only slightly incomplete. You list Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore and Hasan as omitted; that is a long list for a three-person prize, and it is the main reason I do not expect this to be an easy consensus. I accept your argument that B039 and B022 are close in strength, and my preference for B039 rests on its broader scientific consequence and on the five-of-eight top-two support, not on a belief that the clock is flawed.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B039 first as conceptually clean, notes that the concept has spread to photonics and cold atoms, and picks a Bloch, Greiner and Zoller trio for the lattice-simulation candidate while admitting that dropping Cirac is a judgement.
responses.response: I agree with the first part and would build on your point about spread to other platforms, which is good evidence of a concept and not only a material. On B025 I differ somewhat: your trio and my own trio of Bloch, Cirac and Zoller disagree about who to drop, and the fact that members choose different three-name subsets of four credited names tells me that the lattice-simulation candidate is not ready for a clean allocation. I would not rely on it as a second part of a prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can settle on a citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant without appearing to dismiss the BHZ proposal and the 3D topological-insulator discoveries.

Whether the optical lattice clock (B022) should be preferred, since it has equal top-three support and a cleaner two-name credit; the main open point is how much weight to give overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and the pending redefinition of the second.
I cannot verify from the supplied files the priority history among Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and the 3D theorists; I rely on recollection.
My ability to judge condensed-matter theory details is more limited than for detector-centred candidates, so I defer to members with direct expertise.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B039, B022 or B003. My documented collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur, KTH astroparticle group) are not tied to any of the shortlisted candidates. I note only that I ranked B003 first and that neutrino astronomy is a neighbouring astroparticle field, so my earlier preference should be read with that field proximity in mind, although no collaboration with IceCube is recorded in my profile.
